intro: Willem Mengelberg’s Concertgebouw strings slide between notes together and let Mahler’s Adagietto move with a singer’s flexible breath. Made in Amsterdam in 1926, this is a performance by a conductor who knew Mahler and championed his music.

sections.label: A · Harp and sliding strings
sections.mNote: The violin melody leans and moves freely

sections.label: B · Strings carry the flowing middle
sections.mNote: A warm G-string melody moves towards G♭ major

sections.label: A′ · The opening song returns more slowly
sections.mNote: Harp notes reappear beneath the stretched violin phrase

sections.label: A″ · High violins and rising cellos
sections.mNote: The final phrase broadens towards its crest

sections.label: Coda · Strings settle into F major
sections.mNote: The harp stops before the last held chord

cues.title: The melody leans forward
cues.text: Harp and low strings prepare the first violin entry. Mengelberg brings its pickup forward within the bar, giving the phrase a gentle push before it stretches out. The melody breathes unevenly, with small changes of speed inside its long line.
cues.evidence: Jonathan Manton describes the anticipatory opening pickup and flexible pulse in this recording: https://guides.library.yale.edu/c.php?g=525668&p=4452898 . Opening instrumentation: Peters score, plate 9015, p. 178.

cues.title: The whole section slides
cues.text: The strings slide audibly between some notes, moving together as a section. This portamento gives the tune the connected vowels of a singing voice. Mengelberg makes the slides part of the phrase, alongside its pauses and sudden surges.
cues.evidence: Manton’s discussion of this recording identifies coordinated string portamento and abrupt local tempo changes: https://guides.library.yale.edu/c.php?g=525668&p=4452898 . This note describes the performance’s string phrasing across the passage.

cues.title: Mengelberg meets Mahler’s music
cues.text: At Krefeld in 1902, Mengelberg hears Mahler conduct the première of his Third Symphony. He invites him to Amsterdam the following year. The Concertgebouw becomes one of Mahler’s strongest homes, and Mengelberg keeps conducting the music after the composer’s death.
cues.evidence: Manton’s account of Mengelberg’s encounter with Mahler in Krefeld, the 1903 Amsterdam invitation and his later advocacy: https://guides.library.yale.edu/c.php?g=525668&p=4452898

cues.title: The strings move more freely
cues.text: At Fliessender, the harp withdraws and the violins begin a warm melody on the G string. The harmony moves towards G♭ major. The strings carry most of this middle alone, with one brief return of harp arpeggios.
cues.evidence: Peters full score, plate 9015, p. 180: Fliessender, G-Saite, mit Wärme and grosser Ton; harp returns in bars 45–48 before the G♭-major passage. https://s9.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/0/04/IMSLP13083-Mahler-Symphony_No.5_IV.pdf
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: The return takes more time
cues.text: Harp triplets return beneath the held strings, and the first melody begins again. Mengelberg gives this reprise more time than the opening. Its long notes stretch across the bar while the harp keeps placing smaller notes beneath them.
cues.evidence: Manton identifies the slower return in this recording: https://guides.library.yale.edu/c.php?g=525668&p=4452898 . Harp re-entry and Tempo I: Peters score, p. 181.

cues.title: The high phrase broadens
cues.text: The violins climb over rising cellos and harp arpeggios. Mahler asks the strings for broad bow strokes and a full sound; the basses begin to bow beneath them. The phrase opens out before its final descent.
cues.evidence: Peters score, p. 182, final crescendo: breiter Strich, viel Bogen wechseln, viel Ton and arco basses.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Strings finish the song
cues.text: The harp falls silent. Strings descend into the last F-major chord and hold it under a long fermata. In the complete symphony, Mahler asks the Rondo-Finale to begin without a break.
cues.evidence: Peters score, p. 182, final system: harp rests, F-major string ending, long fermatas and attacca Rondo-Finale.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

composer.epithet: A conductor who composed in the summers, and wanted each symphony to hold a whole world — the sublime and the street band together.
facts: Vienna Conservatory, 1875–78: piano with Julius Epstein, composition with Franz Krenn; attended Bruckner’s university lectures
Budapest Royal Opera 1888–91 · Hamburg Stadttheater 1891–97 · Vienna Court Opera 1897–1907 · Metropolitan Opera and New York Philharmonic 1908–11
In summer huts at Steinbach am Attersee, Maiernigg on the Wörthersee, and Toblach in the Dolomites
Nine numbered symphonies and an unfinished Tenth; Das Lied von der Erde; orchestral songs

quote.text: The symphony must be like the world. It must embrace everything.
quote.source: To Jean Sibelius, Helsinki, 1907, as Sibelius remembered it

composer.background:
Mahler was born in a Bohemian village and grew up in the garrison town of Iglau (Jihlava), the second of fourteen children, eight of whom died young. Iglau gave him the sounds that never left his music: bugle calls and marches from the barracks, Czech and German folk song, the town band, the synagogue and the Catholic church. A story he told late in life, to Sigmund Freud, describes running from a violent quarrel between his parents into the street, where a barrel organ was grinding out Ach, du lieber Augustin. Tragedy and the banal, side by side: it is a fair description of half his slow movements.

At fifteen he entered the Vienna Conservatory, studying piano and composition, and sat in on Bruckner’s harmony lectures at the University. His friends were Hugo Wolf and the short-lived Hans Rott, whose symphony sounds so much like Mahler’s own that Mahler later called Rott the founder of the new symphony, as he understood it. The cantata Das klagende Lied, completed in 1880, failed to win the Beethoven Prize in 1881. He had already begun the career that would pay for everything else: conducting.
